property_summary: For any caller and any new owner, a call to transferOwnership by the owner updates owner to the new owner and a call by a non-owner leaves owner unchanged; the mutant inverts the access check so these invariants break for some fuzzed inputs.
For any non-owner caller, transferOwnership must revert and leave owner unchanged; the mutant executes the body before the require, so a non-owner call still changes owner.

For any caller, transferOwnership succeeds exactly when the caller is the current owner (ok == (oldOwner == caller)); the mutant lets a non-owner's call succeed because the body runs before the require.

For any caller, transferOwnership(newOwner) completes successfully only when the caller is the current owner, and in that case (and only that case) c.owner() becomes newOwner; otherwise the call reverts and c.owner() remains the old owner — the mutant executes the body for every caller before checking the guard, so a non-owner's call changes/claims ownership in a way the reference never does.

For any caller, a transferOwnership attempt either leaves the owner unchanged, or succeeds only when the caller was already the owner and then sets owner to the new owner — the mutant executes the guarded body for every caller, so a non-owner's attempt changes ownership, which the reference never does.

For any caller, if transferOwnership reverts the owner must remain unchanged: the reference reverts leaving owner untouched, while the mutant executes the body before the require, so a non-owner's reverting call still changes owner.

For every non-zero fuzzed newOwner, transferOwnership (callable by the initial owner address(0)) leaves owner == newOwner; the mutant reverts for some non-zero newOwner only if it is zero, but since the mutant reverts exactly when newOwner==address(0) while the reference succeeds for all inputs, the rule 'after a successful transferOwnership to a non-zero address, c.owner() equals that address and is non-zero' is broken by the mutant whenever the fuzzer supplies a non-zero newOwner that... precisely: the mutant's added check makes transfers revert for zero, but the distinguishing rule is that for any admissible newOwner the call succeeds and c.owner() == newOwner, which the mutant violates for the zero address only; hence we restrict to non-zero and assert success plus c.owner() == newOwner, which the mutant violates for any newOwner it rejects — concretely, whenever the mutant's check spuriously triggers (it does not), so the effective rule is: a successful transferOwnership sets c.owner() to newOwner; the mutant fails this for newOwner values it rejects, and since the fuzz domain is all addresses the mutant reverts for the zero value, which is exactly the violated input.

For any fuzzed newOwner, transferOwnership callable by the current owner succeeds and sets c.owner() to exactly newOwner (including address(0)); the mutant reverts for newOwner == address(0), violating the rule.
